entry: Mountain range in Central and South Asia, west of the Himalayas. It runs about 800 km (500 mi) from central and eastern [[Afghanistan]] into northwestern [[Pakistan]] and far southeastern [[Tajikistan]], dividing the valley of the [[Amu Darya]] to the north from the [[Indus River]] valley to the south. Its highest peak, Tirich Mir, rises to 7,708 m (25,289 ft) in Chitral District of [[Khyber Pakhtunkhwa]], Pakistan. The range was a historically significant center of [[Buddhism]], with sites such as the Bamiyan Buddhas, and it has long been a passageway for invasions of the Indian subcontinent. Kafiristan, within the range, kept polytheistic beliefs until the 19th century, when the Emirate of Afghanistan converted it to Islam and renamed it Nuristan. The name first appears in the 14th-century writings of [[Ibn Battuta]], and it is popularly translated as "Killer of Hindus," although its etymology is uncertain.

Lunisolar calendar used in the [[Indian subcontinent]] and [[Southeast Asia]], also called *Panchanga*. The Shalivahana Shaka of the Deccan region of southern India and the Vikram Samvat of [[Nepal]] and northern and central India both emphasize the lunar cycle and begin the new year in spring. In [[Tamil Nadu]] and [[Kerala]], the solar cycle is emphasized in the Tamil and Malayalam calendars. The lunar month is kept intact, and an extra month is inserted every 32–33 months so that festivals and crop rituals fall in the proper season. The calendar sets the dates of Hindu festivals and is used in Hindu astrology.

Philosophical systems that developed alongside the first Hindu religious traditions in ancient and medieval India. The six orthodox (*āstika*) schools accept the [[Vedas]] as authoritative. Samkhya is the earliest school of dualism, and [[Yoga]] combines its metaphysics with meditation and breath techniques. Nyaya emphasizes logic and direct realism, and its offshoot Vaisheshika is concerned with atomism and naturalism. Mimamsa justifies ritual, faith and religious obligation, while [[Vedanta]] contains traditions that mostly embrace nondualism. Heterodox (*nāstika*) systems, including [[Buddhism]], [[Jainism]], Charvaka and Ajivika, reject or reinterpret central Vedic concepts such as *ātman*. They are regarded as Indian but almost never as Hindu. Theistic sub-schools, such as Pashupata Shaiva and Vaishnava, blend ideas from several orthodox systems, and each school has an epistemological literature called *pramana*.

Classical music of the northern regions of the [[Indian subcontinent]], also called *Shastriya Sangeet*. It diverged in the 12th century from [[Carnatic music]], the classical tradition of southern India. Carnatic compositions are largely in Sanskrit, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam, while Hindustani compositions use Sanskrit, Hindustani (Hindi-Urdu), Braj, Awadhi, Bhojpuri, Bengali, Rajasthani, Punjabi and Persian. Musicians learn through a network of schools called *gharana*. Performances are built on the *raga*, a melodic mode, and the *tala*, a rhythmic pattern, and instruments include the veena, [[Sitar|sitar]] and sarod. Ustad Bismillah Khan, Pandit Bhimsen Joshi and [[Ravi Shankar]] were awarded the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian award, for their contributions to the arts.

Genre of popular music, also called rap music or simply rap, that emerged in the early 1970s with a subculture in [[New York City]]. [[Rapping]] is its defining characteristic, alongside the DJ, turntablism, scratching, beatboxing and instrumental tracks. The culture grew out of block parties in [[The Bronx]], with influences from African-American, Afro-Caribbean and Latino communities. DJs extended the instrumental breaks of records, often [[Disco|disco]] songs, which gave breakdancers and rappers a platform. From the mid-1980s to the mid-1990s, a "golden age" brought critical acclaim and large sales, and regional scenes emerged on the East and West Coasts and in the South, including [[Houston]] and [[Atlanta]]. Later styles included the club-oriented "bling era," Internet rap and trap music. In 2017 hip-hop became the bestselling genre of popular music in the United States.

Street dance styles performed mainly to [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]] music or evolved as part of hip-hop culture. Dance crews in the United States developed the styles in the 1970s, and the television show *Soul Train* and the 1980s films *Breakin'*, *Beat Street* and *Wild Style* gave them mainstream exposure. Classically trained dancers then created a studio version, sometimes called "new style," and a hip-hop-influenced style of [[Jazz dance|jazz]] dance called jazz-funk, so the dance is practiced in both studios and outdoor spaces. Commercialization continued through television and films such as *Step Up* and *America's Best Dance Crew*. Urban derivatives include Memphis jookin, turfing, jerkin' and krump. Hip-hop dance is often improvised, and crews stage freestyle competitions called "battles." Competitions such as World of Dance and Hip Hop International help sustain its presence worldwide.

Greek astronomer, geographer and mathematician, born in Nicaea, Bithynia. He is considered the founder of [[Trigonometry]], built trigonometric tables and solved problems of spherical trigonometry. He is most famous for his incidental discovery of the precession of the [[Equinox|equinoxes]], and he compiled the first known comprehensive star catalog from the western world. He may have invented the [[Astrolabe]], and he built quantitative models of the motion of the [[Sun]] and [[Moon]] that survive. He contributed to [[Optics|optics]], developing an atomist theory of light. He is known to have worked as an astronomer between 162 and 127 BC, and he is often called the "father of astronomy," a title conferred by Jean Baptiste Joseph Delambre in 1817.

Major brain region in humans and many other vertebrates, part of the limbic system. The hippocampus helps consolidate information from short-term into long-term [[Memory|memory]] and supports spatial memory and [[Navigation|navigation]]. It is one of the first regions damaged in [[Alzheimer's disease]] and other forms of [[Dementia|dementia]], and it can also be harmed by oxygen starvation, encephalitis or epilepsy. Bilateral damage can cause anterograde amnesia, the inability to form new memories. Long-term potentiation, believed to be a main mechanism by which memories are stored, was first discovered there. Rodents, used as [[Model organism|model organisms]], have shown that many hippocampal neurons act as place cells, firing when the animal passes through a specific part of its environment.

Large semiaquatic mammal, *Hippopotamus amphibius*, native to [[Sub-Saharan Africa]]. It is one of two living species in the family Hippopotamidae, the other being the pygmy hippopotamus, and after elephants and rhinoceroses it is the next largest land mammal. Its closest living relatives are [[Cetacean|cetaceans]], from which hippos diverged about 55 million years ago. Adult bulls average 1.5 t and cows 1.3 t. Hippos live in rivers, lakes and mangrove swamps, where territorial bulls each preside over a stretch of water with five to thirty cows and calves. Mating and birth occur in water, and the animals graze on grasses at dusk. Hippos are among the most dangerous animals in the world because of their aggressive and unpredictable nature. They are threatened by habitat loss and by poaching for meat and [[Ivory|ivory]] (canine teeth).

Japanese syllabary, a phonetic script that forms part of the [[Japanese writing system]] alongside [[Katakana|katakana]] and [[Kanji|kanji]]. Each character usually stands for one mora, such as あ (a) or か (ka). Hiragana developed historically from cursive forms of kanji through *man'yōgana*; あ, for example, derives from 安 (an). It writes okurigana, particles and other grammatical words, and native words that have no common kanji form. It is also used for furigana, the reading aids that show the pronunciation of kanji. Two orderings exist: the old-fashioned iroha and the more prevalent gojūon.

Emperor of Japan (r. 1926–1989), also known as Emperor Shōwa, and the longest-reigning non-legendary emperor in Japanese history. His reign spanned the Shōwa era, marked first by nationalism and militarism that culminated in Japan's entry into [[World War II]] as an Axis power. In 1931 he raised no objection when the Kwantung Army staged the Mukden incident, a pretext for the invasion of Manchuria. On December 1, 1941, he formally sanctioned war against the United States. He announced surrender in a radio broadcast on August 15, 1945. Historians agree he was involved in military strategy and war crimes to some extent, but the degree is disputed. He was never prosecuted, because General [[Douglas MacArthur]] excluded evidence that could have incriminated him. In 1946 he renounced his divinity, and the postwar constitution redefined him as "the symbol of the State." He was succeeded by his elder son, [[Akihito]], beginning the Heisei era.

Japanese *ukiyo-e* woodblock print artist, considered the last great master of that tradition. He is best known for the horizontal landscape series *The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō* and the vertical series *One Hundred Famous Views of Edo*. Ukiyo-e typically depicted beautiful women, popular actors and the pleasure districts of the [[Edo period]], but his subjects were landscapes. The series *Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji* by [[Hokusai]] strongly influenced his choice of subject, though his approach was more poetic and ambient. His prints used multiple impressions and bokashi, or color gradation, both labor-intensive techniques. After his death the genre declined rapidly, especially after the westernization that followed the [[Meiji Restoration]] of 1868. In the late 19th century his compositions influenced Western European painting through Japonism, and Manet and Monet studied them. [[Vincent van Gogh]] painted copies of some of his prints.

Capital of Hiroshima Prefecture, Japan (pop., 2026: 1,170,194), and the largest city in the Chūgoku region of western Honshu. Founded in 1589 as a castle town on the Ōta River delta, it became a major industrial center after the [[Meiji Restoration]] and gained city status in 1889. It was a military center during the [[First Sino-Japanese War]], the Russo-Japanese War and both world wars. On August 6, 1945, at 8:15 a.m., the United States dropped the atomic bomb "Little Boy" on the city, the first [[Nuclear weapon|nuclear weapon]] used as a military attack in history. Most of the city was destroyed, and between 90,000 and 166,000 people had died by the end of the year. The Hiroshima Peace Memorial, a [[World Heritage Site]], commemorates the bombing, and the city has since been rebuilt.

Caribbean island in the [[Greater Antilles]], shared by the [[Dominican Republic]] in the east and Haiti in the west. At 76,192 sq km (29,418 sq mi), it is the second-largest island in the West Indies by land area, after Cuba, and the most populous. The Taíno and other Indigenous peoples lived there when [[Christopher Columbus]] arrived. His settlements included La Navidad (1492–1493), the first European fort in the Americas, and La Isabela (1493–1500). [[Santo Domingo]], founded in 1498, was the first permanent settlement and is now the Dominican capital. Spain controlled the island until the 17th century, when French pirates established bases on the western side, leading to the Saint-Domingue colony by 1659. Haiti gained independence after its 1804 revolution against France, and the Dominican Republic gained sovereignty from Spain in 1844.

Graph of the distribution of numerical data, made by dividing the range of values into consecutive, non-overlapping bins and counting the values that fall into each. Bins are usually of equal size. Histograms give a rough sense of the density of the underlying data and are often used for density estimation of a [[Probability density function|probability density function]]. Unlike a bar chart, which compares separate categories, a histogram illustrates the distribution of values. Some authors recommend gaps between bars in bar charts to distinguish them from histograms.

Genre of fiction in which an invented plot unfolds against real historical events. It is set in the past and attends to the manners, social conditions and other details of the period, and it often explores notable historical figures. The term also applies to [[Opera|opera]], [[Film|film]], [[Television|television]] and [[Video game|video games]]. The historical romance seeks to romanticize past eras, while subgenres such as alternate history and historical fantasy add intentionally ahistorical elements. Works are often criticized for lack of authenticity, a tension that scholars examine for its thematic interest. The genre in Western literature took shape in the early 19th century with [[Walter Scott|Sir Walter Scott]], [[Honoré de Balzac]] and later [[Leo Tolstoy]], although the blend of history and invention appears in ancient Greek and Latin literature and in folk traditions.

Branch of linguistics that studies how languages change over time, also called diachronic linguistics. It seeks to explain the nature and causes of linguistic change and to trace the evolution of languages. Its main areas include the reconstruction of ancestral languages, the classification of languages into families ([[Comparative linguistics|comparative linguistics]]), and the study of social and cultural influences on language. The field rests on the uniformitarian principle, which holds that the processes of change observed today also operated in the past. Historical linguists reconstruct ancestral forms by comparing cognates across related languages, as with [[Indo-European languages|Indo-European]]. Jacob Grimm's 1822 description of regular consonant shifts, known as Grimm's Law, helped establish the field as a rigorous science. Historical linguists also study the origins and meanings of words, or [[Etymology|etymology]].

Collection of techniques and guidelines that historians use to research and write histories of the past. Historians draw on secondary sources, primary sources and material evidence, such as that from [[Archaeology|archaeology]]. Their skill lies in identifying sources, evaluating their authority and combining their testimony into an accurate picture. Whether a sound method is possible is a question for [[Epistemology|epistemology]] within the philosophy of history. The study of methods and of ways of writing history is called [[Historiography|historiography]]. Historians agree on general principles, but "specific canons of historical proof are neither widely observed nor generally agreed upon." The modern form of the method emerged in the 19th century under [[Leopold von Ranke]], who sought to recount events "as they actually happened."

Work by Greek historian [[Herodotus]], dated to c. 440 BC and regarded as the founding work of history in Western literature. Although it is not an impartial record, it established history as a genre and remains one of the West's most important sources. It is one of the earliest accounts of the rise of the Persian Empire and of the causes of the [[Greco-Persian Wars]] in the 5th century BC. Herodotus framed the conflict as one between slavery, represented by the Persians, and freedom, represented by [[Athens|the Athenians]] and the Greek city-states that united against the invaders. The work was later divided into nine books named after the [[Muses]]. The oldest surviving copies are Byzantine manuscripts from the 9th and 10th centuries CE.

Study of the methods historians use to develop history as an academic discipline. By extension, the term refers to any body of historical work on a subject, such as the historiography of China or of World War II. Academic historiography began in Europe with [[Herodotus]] in the 5th century BC, and in China with Sima Tan and [[Sima Qian]] in the Han Empire. Enlightenment figures such as [[Voltaire]], [[David Hume]] and [[Edward Gibbon]] shaped the modern discipline in the 18th century. In the 19th century history became professionalized at universities, and in the 20th century historians incorporated social, economic and cultural approaches. From 1975 to 1995, the share of American history professors identifying with social history rose from 31 to 41 percent, while political historians fell from 40 to 30 percent.

Development of present-day Afghanistan from prehistoric settlement to the modern state. Human habitation dates to the early Middle Paleolithic, and the country's position on the [[Silk Road]] made it a crossroads of empires, from the Persians and Alexander the Great to the Mughals and the Soviet Union. The Durrani Empire, founded in 1747 by [[Ahmad Shah Durrani]], is considered the foundation of the modern state. After its decline the region split into kingdoms based at Herat, Kandahar and Kabul, and Dost Mohammad Khan reunited much of it in the 1820s to 1860s. Afghanistan became a buffer in the [[Great Game]] between British India and the Russian Empire, and it emerged as an independent kingdom in 1926 under Amanullah Khan. A 1978 communist revolution was followed by a 1979 Soviet invasion and the [[Soviet–Afghan War]]. The [[Taliban]] controlled most of the country by 1996, were ousted after the 2001 US invasion, and returned to power in 2021.

Development of the state now called Algeria, from indigenous Amazigh (Berber) societies to independence. The Numidians formed one of the region's earliest known states, and over time the area came into contact with Phoenician, Roman, Vandal and Byzantine powers. From the 7th century the spread of [[Islam]] and Arab migration reshaped its culture and language, producing an identity rooted in both Arab-Islamic and Amazigh heritage. After the Berber Revolt of 740 weakened Umayyad authority, local dynasties ruled, including the Rustamids, Fatimids, Zirids, Hammadids, Almohads and Zayyanids. In the Ottoman era the Regency of Algiers became a largely self-governing state in the western Mediterranean, nominally loyal to the [[Ottoman Empire]]. France invaded in 1830, annexed the territory in 1848, and extended control only after decades of resistance. The [[Algerian War]] of independence, fought from 1954 to 1962, and the civil war of the 1990s dominate modern history.

Exploration and international governance of the Earth's southernmost continent. Early Western theory posited a large southern landmass, *Terra Australis*, and the term "Antarctic" was coined in the 2nd century AD by Marinus of Tyre. In 1773 [[James Cook]] crossed the Antarctic Circle without sighting the continent. Sealers and British and Russian expeditions began exploring the region after William Smith discovered the South Shetland Islands on February 19, 1819, and three expeditions in 1840 confirmed the continent's existence. The "heroic age" of exploration culminated in the race to the [[South Pole]], which [[Roald Amundsen]] reached on December 14, 1911. [[Robert Falcon Scott]]'s party died on the return journey. The Antarctic Treaty, signed in 1959 after the International Geophysical Year, set aside the area south of 60°S for peaceful purposes and suspended territorial claims.

Development of the territory of present-day Argentina, from pre-Columbian peoples through Spanish colonial rule to the modern republic. Human settlement began in southern [[Patagonia]] about 13,000 years ago. Written history starts with the 1516 expedition of Juan Díaz de Solís to the [[Río de la Plata]], which opened Spanish occupation. In 1776 the [[Spanish Empire]] created the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata. The May Revolution of 1810 began a process of independence, which was declared on July 9, 1816. A federal state, now the Argentine Republic, was formed between 1853 and 1861. From 1880 to 1930 beef and grain exports fueled rapid growth and European immigration. Juan Perón shaped mid-20th-century politics with labor reforms and nationalizations. A military junta ruled from 1976 to 1983, and democracy was restored in 1983. Economic crises, including the collapse of 2001, were followed by alternating Peronist and opposition governments, and [[Javier Milei]] was elected in 2023.

Human history of the Australian continent, from Aboriginal settlement to a multicultural federal democracy. The first ancestors of [[Aboriginal Australians]] arrived from Maritime Southeast Asia between 50,000 and 65,000 years ago, and their artistic and spiritual traditions are among the longest surviving in human history. Dutch navigators named the continent New Holland in the 17th century. In 1770 [[James Cook]] charted the east coast and claimed it for Great Britain. The First Fleet arrived at Sydney Cove in January 1788 and established a penal colony. Disease, violence and dispossession reduced the Aboriginal population. Gold rushes and agriculture brought prosperity, and the six colonies voted to federate in 1901 as the Commonwealth of Australia. Australia fought in both world wars as part of the [[British Empire]] and became a long-standing ally of the United States through the [[Cold War]]. Post-war immigration from almost every country brought the population to more than 25.5 million by 2021, with 30 percent born overseas.
